species.context: Working execution profile. Taxonomy is source-grounded; ecological claims remain bounded by population, place and evidence.

narrativeChapters.title: A whale is never only a whale.
narrativeChapters.summary: Orcas live through durable social relationships. Their groups can differ in calls, diet, behaviour and habitat use, so a species-level label does not describe every population.

claims.label: Population-specific lives
claims.text: Killer whale populations can have distinct diets, behaviours, social structures and habitat use.
claims.limitation: This is a population-level statement. It must not be used to infer the behaviour of an unidentified individual or occurrence record.

claims.label: Calls carry group identity
claims.text: Some killer whale groups use distinct call structures that help maintain group cohesion and separate social traditions.
claims.limitation: The public prototype does not identify dialect, pod or ecotype from a generic species record.

narrativeChapters.title: What an orca eats depends on who it is.
narrativeChapters.summary: The species has an exceptionally varied diet, but populations and ecotypes often specialise. Food connects the animal to prey, fisheries, habitat quality and human decisions.

claims.label: Specialised foraging
claims.text: Different killer whale populations can specialise in different prey and hunting strategies.
claims.limitation: A GBIF occurrence does not reveal diet, prey availability or ecological condition.

claims.label: A relationship, not a diagnosis
claims.text: Food-web context can help explain why prey and habitat matter, but it is not evidence that a specific observed whale is food-limited.
claims.limitation: 4PLANET interpretation. Requires local population and prey evidence before any stronger public claim.

narrativeChapters.title: A point on a map is a record of observation.
narrativeChapters.summary: Occurrence data can connect a taxon to a reported place and date. It cannot, by itself, establish range, abundance, population trend, live location or ecological health.

claims.label: Accepted taxon identity
claims.text: The prototype preserves the accepted GBIF taxon identity for Orcinus orca across SPECIES and ATLAS.
claims.limitation: Taxonomic acceptance is not a conservation-status or population assessment.

claims.label: Unknown until a record is inspected
claims.text: Population, ecotype, pod, abundance, health and present location remain unknown unless a specific source record supports them.
claims.limitation: Fail-closed rule: the interface must show unknown rather than infer from species identity or map proximity.

narrativeChapters.title: Threats are real — and population-specific.
narrativeChapters.summary: Food limitation, contaminants, vessel disturbance and underwater sound affect some killer whale populations. Responsible action begins by identifying the population, place, evidence and competent actor.

claims.label: Documented pressure categories
claims.text: NOAA identifies food limitations, chemical contaminants, vessel traffic and sound among threats faced by some killer whale populations.
claims.limitation: Do not transfer a threat assessment from one population to another without supporting evidence.

claims.label: No generic intervention claim
claims.text: The prototype does not claim that one universal intervention will protect all orcas.
claims.limitation: A response path requires population-specific science, responsible institutions and an evidence-backed implementation partner.

species.intro: The orca is the largest member of the dolphin family — a fast, social, wide-ranging predator found in every ocean. Populations differ in prey, behaviour and calls, so a species label does not describe every group.
species.habitat: All oceans, from polar seas to the tropics. Coastal groups follow prey along shelves and fjords; others range across open water.

descriptorSource.note: General descriptive summary of identity and habitat; not a measured population or range claim.
